What does Quest Log do?
column2: It tracks staged quests, XP and levels, focus sessions, weekly study goals, monthly activity, and grace days. Data is saved in the browser.

column1: What does each project file do?
column2: index.html supplies structure; styles.css supplies appearance and layout; app.js manages state, events, storage, timers, and DOM updates.

column1: What is the DOM?
column2: The Document Object Model is the browser's tree of objects representing HTML elements and text. JavaScript changes it using DOM APIs.

column1: How does the browser display the app?
column2: It parses HTML, processes CSS, calculates styles, performs layout to determine sizes and positions, and paints. JavaScript changes can trigger further rendering work.

column1: What is application state?
column2: The data describing the app now: XP, quests, weekly target, daily records, and monthly grace usage.

column1: What is the app's main update cycle?
column2: User event → handler → state change → saveState() → render() → browser displays the result.

column1: Does the app have a backend?
column2: No backend is implemented in these files. Logic and persistence are browser-side.

column1: Which state is persistent and which is temporary?
column2: XP, quests, and habit records are saved. Timer variables and toast timeout IDs exist only in memory and disappear on reload.

column1: What does <!doctype html> do?
column2: Requests modern HTML standards mode rather than legacy quirks mode.

column1: What do html, head, and body represent?
column2: html is the document root; head contains metadata and resource links; body contains page content.

column1: What does lang="en" do?
column2: Declares English as the document language, helping assistive technology choose pronunciation.

column1: What does charset="UTF-8" do?
column2: Declares the text encoding so letters, symbols, and emoji are interpreted correctly.

column1: What does the viewport meta tag do?
column2: width=device-width uses the device width for the layout viewport; initial-scale=1.0 sets the initial zoom. This supports mobile layout.

column1: What does title do?
column2: Sets the document title shown in the browser tab and commonly used for bookmarks.

column1: How does the HTML load CSS?
column2: link uses rel="stylesheet" and href="styles.css" to identify and locate the stylesheet.

column1: What is a relative path?
column2: A location resolved relative to the document URL. styles.css and app.js are expected beside index.html.

column1: What is semantic HTML?
column2: Elements used according to meaning, such as header for introductory content, main for primary content, and form for submission controls.

column1: What is the purpose of section and headings?
column2: section groups related content; h1, h2, and h3 express heading hierarchy. The app uses them for its title, sections, and cards.

column1: How do div and span differ?
column2: Both are generic containers. div is block-level and span inline by default; CSS can change their display behavior.

column1: What does strong mean?
column2: It marks important text and is normally bold. The app uses it for changing statistics and emphasized counts.

column1: How is i used here?
column2: It contains weekday markers and colored calendar squares. These uses are mainly visual rather than semantic.

column1: What is an HTML attribute?
column2: A setting on an opening tag, such as id="xp", type="button", or required.

column1: How do id and class differ?
column2: An ID should identify one element uniquely; classes are reusable. JavaScript finds specific controls by ID and CSS styles groups by class.

column1: What does class="btn ghost small" mean?
column2: The element has three classes. btn has no dedicated CSS rule here; button provides the base style, while ghost and small modify it.

column1: What is a Boolean HTML attribute?
column2: Its presence enables a condition. Examples include hidden, required, selected, and disabled.

column1: Why does hidden="false" still mark an element hidden?
column2: Boolean attributes depend on presence, not the text value. JavaScript reveals an element with element.hidden = false.

column1: What is a void element?
column2: An element with no children or closing tag, such as input, meta, or link. The trailing slash in input markup is optional in HTML.

column1: How are HTML comments written?
column2: <!-- comment -->. They document source code and are not displayed as page content.

column1: How does label associate with a control?
column2: Its for attribute can match the control's ID, or the control can be nested inside the label. Clicking the label can focus or activate the control.

column1: What does aria-label do?
column2: Supplies an accessible name. The target select is named Study days per week.

column1: How do select, option, value, and selected work together?
column2: select provides a menu; option supplies choices; value supplies each choice's data; selected establishes the initial choice, which JavaScript can later override.

column1: Why convert targetSelect.value with Number()?
column2: Form control values are strings. Number() converts the selected digits to a number for calculations.

column1: How do button and submit types differ?
column2: type="button" performs ordinary scripted actions; type="submit" submits its form. Explicit types prevent accidental submission.

column1: What do required, maxlength, and placeholder do?
column2: required activates empty-field validation; maxlength limits normal text entry; placeholder displays an example while empty, without becoming the value.

column1: Why use a form to add quests?
column2: It supports native validation and Enter-key submission. JavaScript intercepts submit to add a quest without navigating.

column1: Why are several HTML containers empty initially?
column2: active-list, done-list, week-chips, and heatmap receive child elements generated from JavaScript state.

column1: Why load app.js at the end of body?
column2: Earlier elements have already been parsed, so the script can find them immediately without waiting for DOMContentLoaded.

column1: What is the difference between const and let?
column2: const prevents reassignment of its binding; let permits reassignment. Both are block-scoped.

column1: Does const make an object immutable?
column2: No. const rec = { minutes: 0 } permits rec.minutes = 25, but prevents assigning rec to another object.

column1: What is block scope?
column2: A let or const variable is accessible inside its enclosing block and nested blocks, subject to declaration and initialization rules.

column1: Which value types does the app use?
column2: Strings for titles and IDs, numbers for XP and minutes, Booleans for flags, null for explicit absence, and objects and arrays for structured data.

column1: How do null and undefined differ?
column2: null explicitly represents absence. undefined commonly comes from missing properties, unsuccessful find(), or a function without a returned value.

column1: What is an object?
column2: A collection of named properties, such as { title: "Study", status: "active" }.

column1: What is an array?
column2: An ordered collection indexed from zero. state.quests contains quest objects, and names[0] reads the first stage name.

column1: How do dot and bracket notation differ?
column2: quest.title uses a fixed property name. rec[habitFlag] uses the value of a variable as the name; if habitFlag is "review", it accesses rec.review.

column1: What does { name } mean?
column2: Object property shorthand for { name: name }.

column1: What can braces mean in JavaScript?
column2: An object literal, such as { done: false }, or a statement block, such as an if or function body. Context determines meaning.

column1: How do parameters and arguments differ?
column2: Parameters are names in a function definition. Arguments are actual values passed in a call.

column1: What does return do?
column2: Ends the current function and optionally supplies a result. return; produces undefined.

column1: What is an arrow function?
column2: A compact function expression using =>. s => s.done returns the done property of its argument.

column1: How do arrow function returns work?
column2: An expression body returns implicitly. A block body needs an explicit return to supply a value.

column1: Why wrap an object in parentheses in an arrow return?
column2: (name, i) => ({ id: i, name }) treats braces as an object expression rather than a function body.

column1: What is a callback?
column2: A function supplied to another function or API for execution, such as an event handler, timer callback, or map callback.

column1: What is a closure?
column2: A function retaining access to its surrounding lexical scope. () => useGraceDay(key) remembers the date key for its chip.

column1: How do startTimer and startTimer() differ?
column2: startTimer refers to the function; startTimer() executes it and produces its return value. Listeners need a function reference or wrapper.

column1: How do =, ===, and !== differ?
column2: = assigns; === tests strict equality without coercion; !== tests strict inequality. "5" === 5 is false.

column1: What do += and ++ do?
column2: x += n adds n and stores the result; x++ increments by one. They update XP, minutes, and counts.

column1: What does % do?
column2: Gives the remainder after division. totalSec % 60 obtains seconds remaining after full minutes.

column1: What do ! and !! do?
column2: ! logically negates; !! converts a value to Boolean. stage.done = !stage.done flips a completion flag.

column1: What values are falsy?
column2: false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, and NaN are examples. Empty arrays and objects are truthy.

column1: How do logical AND and OR work?
column2: AND stops at a falsy operand; OR stops at a truthy operand. They return operand values rather than necessarily Booleans. This enables safe checks and fallback values.

column1: What is short-circuit evaluation?
column2: Skipping further evaluation when the result is determined. rec && rec.focus avoids accessing focus when rec is null.

column1: What is the ternary operator?
column2: condition ? a : b chooses a if truthy and b otherwise, producing a value.

column1: What does typeof do?
column2: Returns a type-name string. Arrays also report "object", so use Array.isArray() to identify arrays.

column1: What does unary + do to a Date?
column2: Converts it to a numeric timestamp. +d === +today compares exact instants, not calendar dates.

column1: What is a template literal?
column2: A backtick-delimited string with interpolation using ${expression}, such as `${minutes} min logged`.

column1: What do trim(), toLowerCase(), and includes() do?
column2: trim removes surrounding whitespace; toLowerCase returns lowercase text; includes checks a substring. They do not understand linguistic meaning.

column1: What do slice(0, 7) and padStart(2, "0") do?
column2: slice extracts indexes 0 through 6; padStart adds leading zeroes until at least two characters. They build month keys and padded dates.

column1: What do String() and Number() do?
column2: Convert values to text and numbers respectively. Number() can produce NaN if conversion fails.

column1: How do if, else if, and else work?
column2: They choose branches by conditions; the first satisfied branch runs. else handles remaining cases.

column1: What is a guard clause?
column2: An early return that rejects an invalid situation before the main work, such as if (!quest) return.

column1: How do for...of and a counter-based for loop differ?
column2: for...of visits collection values; a counter loop initializes, tests, and increments an index to control iterations.

column1: How do break and continue differ?
column2: break exits a loop; continue skips the remaining current iteration and proceeds to the next.

column1: What do try and catch do?
column2: try contains code that may throw; catch handles the exception. loadState uses this to recover from storage or JSON errors.

column1: What does map() do?
column2: Returns a new array of transformed items. active.map(renderQuest) creates one article per active quest.

column1: What does filter() do?
column2: Returns a new array of items passing a callback test. It separates quest statuses and removes selected quests.

column1: What does find() do?
column2: Returns the first matching item or undefined. It locates quests and stages by ID.

column1: What does every() do?
column2: Tests whether all items pass. allStagesDone uses it; an empty array also returns true.

column1: What do forEach() and unshift() do?
column2: forEach executes a callback per item and returns undefined; unshift mutates an array by inserting at the beginning.

column1: What does Array.from({ length: 7 }, (_, i) => ...) do?
column2: Creates seven items with indexes 0–6. The underscore is an ordinary name indicating an unused parameter.

column1: How does spread syntax work in objects and calls?
column2: { ...rec, grace: false } copies and overrides properties. replaceChildren(...chips) expands an array into individual arguments.

column1: How are JavaScript comments written?
column2: // is a line comment; /* ... */ can span lines; /** ... */ is documentation-style but remains a comment.

column1: What does getElementById() return?
column2: The matching DOM element or null. Renaming an HTML ID without updating JavaScript can cause property access errors.

column1: What does createElement() do?
column2: Creates a detached element in memory; inserting it into the document makes it part of the page.

column1: What does querySelector() do?
column2: Returns the first matching element in the searched scope. card.querySelector searches descendants within that card.

column1: What does textContent do, and why use it for titles?
column2: Sets text without parsing HTML. User titles are displayed literally, avoiding HTML injection through that assignment.

column1: How do className and classList differ?
column2: className replaces the class string. classList allows individual additions and removals without replacing other classes.

column1: What does classList.toggle("is-done", done) do?
column2: Forces the class present when done is true and absent when false.

column1: How do appendChild() and replaceChildren() differ?
column2: appendChild adds or moves a node to the end; replaceChildren replaces all existing children with supplied nodes or text.

column1: What do setAttribute() and element.style.width do?
column2: setAttribute changes a named HTML attribute; style.width assigns inline CSS, normally overriding ordinary stylesheet width declarations.

column1: What do value, hidden, disabled, and checked represent?
column2: Current control value, hidden state, disabled state, and current checkbox selection. JavaScript changes these DOM properties to update the UI.

column1: How do the checked attribute and property differ?
column2: The attribute describes initial checked state; the checked property reflects current state. Generated checkboxes receive their current state from saved data.

column1: What is an event listener?
column2: A callback registered to execute when the browser dispatches an event, such as click, change, or submit.

column1: What does preventDefault() do in the form handler?
column2: Cancels default form submission and navigation, allowing a local state update instead.

column1: What is localStorage?
column2: Browser string key-value storage associated with an origin and generally retained across reloads. It does not automatically synchronize across devices.

column1: What is an origin?
column2: For ordinary web URLs, the combination of scheme, hostname, and port. Storage is separated by origin.

column1: Why use JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse()?
column2: stringify converts state into text for storage; parse reconstructs data. Invalid JSON throws an exception.

column1: Are localStorage operations asynchronous?
column2: No, they are synchronous. The current execution waits for them to complete.

column1: What does emptyState() create?
column2: A fresh state object with zero XP, no quests, a target of five, and empty daily-record and monthly-grace maps.

column1: Why create fresh default objects?
column2: To avoid accidentally sharing mutable arrays or objects between separate default-state instances.

column1: How does loadState() recover from failures?
column2: It returns defaults for absent data, invalid top-level quests data, or exceptions during storage access and parsing.

column1: Does loadState() fully validate saved data?
column2: No. It does not thoroughly validate quest stages, numeric XP, target range, or day records. Malformed data can pass initial checks.

column1: What risk exists in saveState()?
column2: It lacks exception handling. A failed storage write can interrupt the handler after in-memory mutation and before rendering.

column1: How is the level calculated?
column2: Math.floor(xp / 50) + 1. Levels increase every fifty total XP, starting at level one.

column1: How does dayKey() identify a day?
column2: Uses local year, month plus one, and day, padded into YYYY-MM-DD. Local getters avoid confusing the local day with a UTC date.

column1: How does startOfWeek() calculate Monday?
column2: Copies the date at midnight, converts Sunday-first weekday numbering with (getDay() + 6) % 7, and subtracts the offset.

column1: Why copy dates and use setDate()?
column2: Dates are mutable; copies protect inputs. setDate performs calendar arithmetic with month/year overflow rather than assuming every day is exactly 24 hours.

column1: What does ensureDay() create?
column2: A stored day record with minutes: 0 and false focus, review, practice, and grace flags, then returns that mutable record.

column1: What makes a day active?
column2: Any activity flag, grace flag, or positive minutes. Several sessions still count as one active day.

column1: What does logActivity() do?
column2: Adds credited minutes, marks the habit flag, adds ten XP, saves, renders, and shows a toast. It returns whether the flag was newly completed.

column1: Does logActivity() award XP only once daily?
column2: No. Every call awards ten XP; firstTime only controls first completion marking and notification wording.

column1: How do grace days affect rewards?
column2: They count as active days toward the weekly goal, but add neither study minutes nor XP.

column1: Which month is charged for a grace day?
column2: The month of the selected date, not necessarily the current month. Each month permits two.

column1: What issue arises from parsing grace dates at noon?
column2: Today's noon is in the future before noon and in the past afterward, so eligibility depends on the time if today is mistakenly offered as missed.

column1: How does startTimer() work?
column2: Rejects an already-running timer, stores Date.now() plus twenty-five minutes in milliseconds, updates controls, and schedules 250-millisecond UI updates.

column1: Why use a finish timestamp?
column2: Browser interval callbacks may be delayed. Subtracting current time from the intended finish time avoids accumulating counter drift.

column1: What is the event loop's relevance to timers?
column2: Callbacks run when scheduling and current execution allow. Requested delays are not exact guarantees, especially in background tabs.

column1: How is the countdown formatted?
column2: Remaining milliseconds are rounded upward to seconds; floor(seconds / 60) gives minutes, remainder modulo sixty gives seconds, and padding gives MM:SS.

column1: How do cancellation and completion differ?
column2: Cancellation clears the timer without rewards. Completion clears it and records twenty-five focus minutes plus ten XP.

column1: What happens if a session crosses midnight or the page reloads?
column2: Completion is credited to its finish date. Reloading loses an unfinished timer because it is not persisted.

column1: Do review and practice buttons contain actual exercises?
column2: No. Each immediately credits ten minutes and ten XP, without showing flashcards/questions or verifying completion.

column1: Which actions can repeat daily?
column2: Focus can repeat and earns rewards per finished session. Review and practice are disabled by the UI after their first daily completion.

column1: How does goalStats() count progress?
column2: It visits the current Monday-first week up to today and counts active day records, not total sessions.

column1: How is the progress bar percentage calculated?
column2: Rounded done/target × 100, capped at 100. The displayed completed-day count can exceed the target.

column1: How does renderGoal() build weekday chips?
column2: Maps dates to detached buttons or spans, assigns state classes and markers, attaches grace callbacks, then inserts all chips with replaceChildren.

column1: What is the today bug in renderGoal()?
column2: Week dates are midnight while today includes the current time, so an inactive current date usually enters the missed branch. Exact timestamp equality does not identify the calendar day.

column1: How could the today bug be fixed?
column2: Normalize both values to local midnight or compare dayKey values consistently for calendar-day equality and ordering.

column1: How do minutes map to heatmap intensity?
column2: Zero or fewer: l0; 1–24: l1; 25–49: l2; 50–74: l3; 75 or more: l4. CSS determines colors.

column1: How is the month's length found?
column2: new Date(year, month + 1, 0).getDate() requests day zero of next month, meaning the final day of the current month.

column1: Why does the calendar add blank cells?
column2: To align the first day to its weekday and complete the final week. Hidden visibility preserves their grid positions.

column1: How is totalCells calculated?
column2: Ceiling of (leading offset + days in month) / 7, multiplied by 7, creates complete week columns.

column1: How does the monthly summary format duration?
column2: Totals minutes, divides downward by sixty for hours, and uses remainder for leftover minutes.

column1: What limitation affects a grace-only monthly summary?
column2: Active days may exist but minutes remain zero; the summary condition therefore reports no sessions logged. Grace tooltips also say no study.

column1: How does renderActions() communicate completion?
column2: Toggles is-done, switches explanatory/completed paragraphs, disables review/practice, and restores timer controls when no timer runs.

column1: How does makeStages() select stages?
column2: Lowercases the title and checks study, cleaning, then exercise substrings; otherwise uses generic stages. First matching category wins.

column1: What limitations affect keyword stage generation?
column2: Substring checks do not understand meaning or word boundaries. Words can match inside unrelated words and category order affects results.

column1: How are quest IDs generated, and what is the risk?
column2: Date.now().toString() gives a timestamp string. Two creations in one millisecond can collide.

column1: What does the submit handler do in order?
column2: Prevent submission, trim/check title, prepend a new quest, clear input, save state, render.

column1: What does toggleStage() do?
column2: Finds an active quest and matching stage, flips done, saves, and renders. It rejects missing records and completed quests.

column1: What does completeQuest() check and change?
column2: Verifies active status and all completed stages, changes status to done, adds thirty XP, saves, and renders.

column1: Why validate completion when the button is already disabled?
column2: UI restrictions are not sufficient validation. Function-level guards protect the data operation and prevent repeated completion rewards.

column1: Does the final stage automatically complete a quest?
column2: No. It enables Complete; the user must click that button to receive XP and move the quest to Completed.

column1: Does quest completion update study activity?
column2: No. It changes status and XP without logging habit minutes or updating a day record.

column1: How does deleteQuest() work?
column2: Replaces the quests array with a filtered array excluding the chosen ID, saves, and renders. Only active cards display Delete, but the function itself has no status restriction.

column1: How does renderQuest() create a card?
column2: Creates an article and heading, labeled stage checkboxes, and either active action buttons or a completion badge; returns the detached article.

column1: Why disable completed stage checkboxes?
column2: Completed quests are final in the UI. toggleStage also rejects completed quests, enforcing the restriction in logic.

column1: Why is the hardcoded +30 XP label a maintenance issue?
column2: If XP_PER_QUEST changes, the label can become inaccurate. Deriving it from the constant keeps display and reward consistent.

column1: What does render() update?
column2: XP and level, weekly goal, action cards, heatmap, both quest lists, and empty-state message visibility.

column1: What is the cost of rebuilding quest lists?
column2: New nodes and listeners are created on each render. It is simple for a small app but can lose focus when the active control is replaced.

column1: Does the interface refresh automatically at midnight?
column2: No dedicated refresh exists. Daily information can stay stale until another action triggers rendering or the page reloads.

column1: Why can earlier-declared functions reference state initialized later?
column2: Their bodies execute after state initialization. Declaring a function does not immediately execute it.

column1: What does the final render() call do?
column2: Populates the initial interface from loaded state after DOM references and listeners are ready.

column1: How does showToast() protect newer messages?
column2: Clears the earlier hide timeout before scheduling a new one, restarting the visible period for the newest message.

column1: How does CSS style elements created later by JavaScript?
column2: Rules match the current DOM, including dynamically inserted nodes. Generated quest, stage, badge, and chip classes receive existing styles.

column1: Why can hidden fail for the goal badge?
column2: An author display: inline-block rule can override default hidden styling. An explicit .goal-badge[hidden] display: none rule would enforce it.

column1: How is the toast centered and layered?
column2: Fixed positioning anchors it to the viewport; left: 50% plus translateX(-50%) centers it; z-index and shadow place it visually above content.

column1: Why use labels around stage checkboxes?
column2: They associate text with controls, enlarge the clickable area, and provide accessible names.

column1: What accessibility limitations exist?
column2: Progress lacks progress semantics, heatmap details rely on hover titles, toast changes lack a live region, and DOM replacement can disrupt keyboard focus.

column1: What persistence limitations exist?
column2: Storage is browser-local, can be cleared, has no device synchronization, receives partial validation, and does not preserve timers.

column1: Which improvements most affect correctness?
column2: Fix calendar-day comparisons, enforce hidden badge styling, validate loaded data, handle storage failures, and refresh daily state after date changes.

column1: How could review/practice labels match functionality better?
column2: Implement real exercises and record verified completion, or rename the buttons to indicate self-reported activity logging.

column1: How would you explain the architecture in a viva?
column2: A client-side, event-driven application with structured state, local persistence, and explicit render functions. HTML supplies containers, JavaScript manages behavior, and CSS styles the resulting DOM.

column1: Trace adding and completing Study maths across the files.
column2: The form collects text; JavaScript generates study stages and saves the quest; renderQuest builds controls; CSS styles them; change events update stages; Complete awards XP and render moves the card.

column1: Why discuss actual behavior rather than just UI wording?
column2: Code determines behavior. Explaining immediate credits, date issues, and persistence limits demonstrates implementation understanding.

column1: How should you answer a viva execution question?
column2: Name the trigger, identify the handler, explain the state mutation, describe persistence, then explain DOM changes and the visible result.
